> 「当何名此经？我等云何奉持？」「是经名为《金刚般若波罗蜜》，以是名字，汝当奉持。……佛说般若波罗蜜，即非般若波罗蜜，是名般若波罗蜜。」

The thirteenth section is where the sutra names itself — and immediately applies its own formula to the name.

金刚般若波罗蜜: the diamond of prajñā that carries you across. 金刚, unbreakable and sharp, able to cut through affliction. 般若, the seeing that is free of marks, distinct from cleverness. 波罗蜜, gone to the other shore.

Then: what is called prajñā-pāramitā is not prajñā-pāramitā, therefore it is called prajñā-pāramitā.

## 奉持 is holding the meaning, not the word

须菩提 asks how to uphold it. The answer gives the name, then dissolves it.

The book reads this as a warning built into the sutra's own title page: reciting "diamond prajñā pāramitā" while the mind keeps grasping a thing called prajñā, and a place called the other shore, is holding a name rather than a teaching.

A name is an identifier. 奉持 happens in the mind, in how a sentence is allowed to work on you. This is the same distinction as section eight's 受持: receiving plus holding, over time, until it changes what you do.

## 如来无所说

Asked whether the Tathāgata has taught anything, 须菩提 says: nothing.

The Buddha does not correct him. This is not a claim that the sutras are later fabrications. Speech appears and functions; it guides, it corrects, it points. What is denied is a fixed dharma-body being transferred through words — as if a sentence could carry the thing itself in its pocket.

The book's image: a finger at the moon. The finger works. It just isn't the moon, and no one who has seen the moon keeps looking at the finger.

## 微尘 and 世界

The section then takes the largest and smallest units available: the dust-particles that make up a world, and the world they make up. Both are subjected to the formula.

Not nonexistent — that is the misreading the book spends the most space correcting. What is denied is a permanent, independent entity. Dust arises from conditions and disperses; a world holds together for a while and comes apart. The appearance functions; the substance does not hold.

Which is exactly why one can work in the world without being owned by it. The world is neither solid nor nothing. It is workable.

## 身命布施 and the direction of the comparison

The section closes by measuring again: even giving one's body and life — the heaviest gift in the old scale, beyond treasure — does not compare with receiving this sutra.

The book's guardrail: this is a comparison of freedom from grasping, not a ranking of compassion. Giving one's body while holding the transaction is still 有为. Explaining the sutra while hoping for a large return is the same error on the other side.

## The test

Take the name of your own practice. The word you use for what you are doing — meditation, study, service, craft.

Say it, then check what you are holding when you say it. A method? An identity? A promise about where it takes you?

The name is fine. The sutra's own name did not survive its formula either.
